_about: Bag interaction checks. Conservative, well-established pairs only; every warning tells the shopper to check with the pharmacist, and the pharmacist sees the same warnings on the order. Classes match an ingredient (lower-cased, from products.generics) by regular expression. A rule whose classes are the same fires when two different products in the bag both fall in that class. Topical/eye/ear forms are ignored (see InteractionChecker::SYSTEMIC_FORMS).

rules.title: Paracetamol in more than one product
rules.detail: Taking these together can push you over the safe daily amount of paracetamol, which can damage the liver.
rules.advice: Use only one paracetamol-containing product at a time, and don't take more than 4 g (8 × 500 mg) in 24 hours.

rules.title: Two anti-inflammatory painkillers
rules.detail: Two NSAIDs together raise the risk of stomach bleeding and kidney problems without giving better pain relief.
rules.advice: Take only one of these at a time unless a doctor told you otherwise.

rules.title: Blood thinner with an anti-inflammatory painkiller
rules.detail: Together they significantly raise the risk of serious bleeding, including in the stomach.
rules.advice: Don't combine these without your doctor's advice. Paracetamol is usually the safer painkiller with a blood thinner.

rules.title: Blood thinner with an antiplatelet
rules.detail: Both stop blood from clotting in different ways; together the bleeding risk is much higher.
rules.advice: Only take both if a doctor prescribed them together.

rules.title: Two blood thinners
rules.detail: Two anticoagulants together can cause dangerous bleeding.
rules.advice: These are normally never taken together. Check with your doctor or our pharmacist.

rules.title: Antiplatelet with an anti-inflammatory painkiller
rules.detail: The combination raises the risk of stomach bleeding.
rules.advice: Ask the pharmacist about a safer painkiller or stomach protection.

rules.title: Warfarin with metronidazole
rules.detail: Metronidazole strongly increases the effect of warfarin and the risk of bleeding.
rules.advice: Your INR needs closer checks; tell the doctor who manages your warfarin.

rules.title: Erectile-dysfunction medicine with a nitrate
rules.detail: This combination can cause a sudden, dangerous drop in blood pressure.
rules.advice: Never take these together.

rules.title: Antidepressant with tramadol
rules.detail: Together they can cause serotonin syndrome (agitation, fever, shaking) and raise the risk of seizures.
rules.advice: Check with your doctor before using tramadol with this antidepressant.

rules.title: Two antidepressants of the same kind
rules.detail: Two SSRI/SNRI medicines together can cause serotonin syndrome.
rules.advice: These are usually not taken together; only do so if a doctor is switching you between them.

rules.title: Antidepressant with a migraine triptan
rules.detail: There is a small risk of serotonin syndrome.
rules.advice: Usually fine at normal doses; stop and get help if you feel agitated, feverish or shaky.

rules.title: Tramadol with a sedative
rules.detail: Opioid painkillers with sedatives can cause deep drowsiness and slowed breathing.
rules.advice: Avoid this combination unless a doctor prescribed both.

rules.title: Two sedatives
rules.detail: Together they can cause excessive drowsiness and slowed breathing.
rules.advice: Take only one unless prescribed; don't drive.

rules.title: Antibiotic with an antacid, iron, calcium or zinc
rules.detail: These minerals stop the antibiotic from being absorbed, so it may not work.
rules.advice: Take the antibiotic at least 2 hours before or 4–6 hours after the mineral product.

rules.title: Thyroid tablet with an antacid, iron or calcium
rules.detail: These reduce how much levothyroxine your body absorbs.
rules.advice: Take levothyroxine on an empty stomach, at least 4 hours apart from these.

rules.title: Blood-pressure medicine with a potassium-raising medicine
rules.detail: Together they can raise potassium to dangerous levels.
rules.advice: Only combine these with a doctor's supervision and blood tests.

rules.title: Blood-pressure medicine with an anti-inflammatory painkiller
rules.detail: NSAIDs can weaken blood-pressure control and strain the kidneys.
rules.advice: Use the NSAID for as short a time as possible, drink enough water, or ask about paracetamol.

rules.title: Domperidone with a macrolide or azole
rules.detail: This combination can cause a dangerous heart-rhythm problem (QT prolongation).
rules.advice: Don't take these together; ask the pharmacist for an alternative.

rules.title: Two anti-sickness medicines that affect heart rhythm
rules.detail: Both can lengthen the QT interval.
rules.advice: Use one at a time unless your doctor advised both.

rules.title: Statin with clarithromycin, itraconazole or ketoconazole
rules.detail: The statin level rises sharply, which can cause serious muscle damage.
rules.advice: Your doctor may pause the statin while you take the other medicine.

rules.title: Digoxin with a medicine that raises it
rules.detail: Digoxin can build up to toxic levels (sickness, slow or irregular heartbeat).
rules.advice: Tell the doctor who prescribes your digoxin before starting this.

rules.title: Methotrexate with an anti-inflammatory painkiller
rules.detail: NSAIDs can raise methotrexate to toxic levels.
rules.advice: Check with your doctor before using an NSAID.

rules.title: Two antihistamines
rules.detail: Doubling up adds drowsiness and side effects without better relief.
rules.advice: Use one antihistamine at a time.

rules.title: Two oral decongestants
rules.detail: Together they can raise blood pressure and heart rate.
rules.advice: Use only one decongestant product.
